The Purple sea urchin Paracentrotus lividus exhibits a well-defined test diameter at settlement of 0.048 centimeters , marking the transition from a planktonic larva to a benthic juvenile. This metric was recorded for individuals that reached metamorphic competence and subsequently attached to the substratum, a critical bottleneck in early survival. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 19.5 °C [T = 19.5 °C], the time since birth at settlement was documented as 18 days , reflecting the rapid development of the pluteus larva through its planktotrophic feeding phase. These free-swimming larvae rely on phytoplankton grazing to accumulate sufficient energy reserves for the profound morphological transformation that occurs at settlement. The small size at this stage, equivalent to just a few hundred microns across the test, underscores the vulnerability of newly settled recruits to predation and abiotic stressors. This early life history parameter is consistent with values reported for other Mediterranean echinoids, linking larval duration directly to thermal conditions that govern metabolic and developmental rates during the exotrophic period.

Feeding rates in Paracentrotus lividus show a pronounced size dependency, as demonstrated by laboratory measurements of ingestion at a stable temperature of 19.5 °C [T = 19.5 °C]. For a very small juvenile with a wet body mass of only 0.006 grams, the daily feeding rate was recorded as 0.082 grams per day , a modest intake reflecting the limited foraging capacity and small gut volume of newly metamorphosed individuals at a temperature of 19.5 °C [T = 19.5 °C]. In striking contrast, a substantially larger specimen weighing 4.45 grams exhibited a feeding rate of 0.288 grams per day , representing a more than threefold increase in ingestion that scales with the demands of somatic growth and gonadal development at a temperature of 19.5 °C [T = 19.5 °C]. These rates were derived from controlled algal consumption experiments in flow-through aquaria, with the water temperature held constant to isolate the effect of body size on food processing. Such allometric variation in feeding intensity is typical of grazing echinoids and plays a direct role in determining how quickly juveniles can progress toward the test diameter at puberty.

The ultimate test diameter, or asymptotic adult size, of Paracentrotus lividus has been estimated at 6.5 centimeters [Li = 6.5 centimeters], a value that represents the maximum horizontal dimension of the calcareous test in fully grown individuals. This species is among the larger regular echinoids found in shallow Mediterranean and eastern Atlantic habitats, where it occupies rocky substrates and seagrass meadows. Field surveys of mature populations indicate that individuals approaching this size are typically several years old and have invested heavily in both somatic growth and reproductive tissue. In contrast, the onset of sexual maturation is defined by a much smaller test diameter at puberty of 2.25 centimeters [Lp = 2.25 centimeters], a threshold at which individuals first develop functional gonads and become capable of participating in annual spawning events. This size-based transition from a sub-adult to a reproductively active adult is a common life history pattern among echinoids, decoupling the timing of first reproduction from chronological age, which can vary with food availability and thermal regime.

For females from a specific cohort tracked over 172 days, the maximum recorded gonadosomatic index (GSI) reached 16% [GSI = 16%] under a thermal regime of 14.5 °C [T = 14.5 °C]. This value, representing one of the highest observed for this species, indicates a substantial allocation of resources toward gamete production during the pre-spawning period. The cooler temperature likely contributes to an extended window of vitellogenesis, allowing for more complete ovarian maturation before the onset of spawning. Understanding the environmental drivers of this metric is important for fishery management, as the gonads of Paracentrotus lividus are a highly valued seafood product in many Mediterranean regions, and their yield varies seasonally with reproductive condition.

The maximum life span of Paracentrotus lividus has been estimated at 3285 days [am = 3285 days], equivalent to approximately nine years, based on long-term field observations and tag-recapture studies conducted at a mean water temperature of 19.5 °C [T = 19.5 °C]. This longevity places the species among the longer-lived regular echinoids, with individuals potentially surviving for nearly a decade in stable, low-predation environments. The extended life span is accompanied by persistent reproductive activity across multiple seasons, as sexually mature adults continue to spawn annually once they have surpassed the test diameter at puberty. This life history strategy, characterized by gradual, indeterminate growth and repeated spawning events, is well-suited to the relatively stable, oligotrophic conditions of Mediterranean subtidal habitats. In comparison to faster-growing echinoids from more productive or colder waters, Paracentrotus lividus trades rapid turnover for a longer reproductive window, investing in durable skeletal structures and regular gamete production over many years. The capacity to reach an advanced age also underscores the importance of post-settlement survival and the role of habitat complexity in providing refugia from predators.
